A.q: Which statement correctly describes the position and shape of the heart?
options: It lies slightly left of centre in the chest and is pear-shaped or an inverted cone.
It lies slightly right of centre in the chest and is spherical or a rounded cone.
It lies centrally behind the sternum and is oval-shaped or a flattened cone.
It lies low in the abdomen and is bean-shaped or a curved cone.
A.explain: The heart lies slightly left of centre in the chest and is described as pear-shaped or an inverted cone. Positions to the right, centrally behind the sternum, or low in the abdomen do not match its anatomical location, and spherical, oval, or bean shapes do not match its gross form.

A.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the heart from the blood vessels?
options: The heart delivers blood to the lungs and body, while the blood vessels pump blood out to the heart and back again
The heart pumps blood out to the lungs and body, while the blood vessels deliver and receive blood to and from the body
The heart receives blood from the lungs and body, while the blood vessels pump blood out to the heart and back again
The heart regulates one-way flow through valves, while the blood vessels contract to produce body heat and movement
A.explain: The heart is the muscular pump sending blood to the lungs and body, while arteries and veins are the vessels that deliver and receive blood to and from the body. Describing the heart as a receiver or regulator of one-way flow, or assigning pumping to the vessels, reverses the roles; blood vessels do not generate the main propulsive force of circulation.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the cardiac chambers and septa?
options: The atria are the lower chambers, the ventricles are the upper chambers, and the septa join the right and left sides.
The atria are the upper chambers, the ventricles are the lower chambers, and the septa join the right and left sides.
The atria are the upper chambers, the ventricles are the lower chambers, and the septa partition the right and left sides.
The atria are the lower chambers, the ventricles are the upper chambers, and the septa partition the right and left sides.
A.explain: Atria are upper chambers, ventricles are lower chambers, and septa partition the right and left sides. Calling atria lower or ventricles upper reverses chamber position, and saying septa join rather than partition sides misstates their role.

A.q: Which sequence lists the heart wall layers from outer to inner?
A.explain: From outer to inner, the wall runs epicardium, myocardium, endocardium. The epicardium is the outer layer, the myocardium the middle muscle layer, and the endocardium the inner lining. Other orders place the muscle layer outside the epithelial lining or put the endocardium superficial to the myocardium.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the pericardium and its parts?
options: The pericardium is a two-layered sac with fluid between, the visceral layer lies closest to the heart, and the parietal layer forms the outer wall.
The pericardium is a single muscular wall of the heart, the visceral layer lines the chambers, and the parietal layer covers the valves and septa.
The pericardium is a fluid cavity within the ventricles, the visceral layer forms the outer sac, and the parietal layer lies closest to the heart muscle.
The pericardium is a one-way valve at the aorta, the visceral layer opens with systole, and the parietal layer closes during diastole and relaxation.
A.explain: The pericardium is a two-layered protective sac with fluid in the pericardial cavity. The visceral pericardium is the layer closest to the heart, corresponding to the epicardium, and the parietal pericardium lines the outer wall. Descriptions that make it a single muscular wall, an internal ventricular cavity, or an aortic valve confuse it with heart wall layers or valves.

A.q: Which statement correctly defines heart valves?
options: They are partitions between the right and left atria that prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
They are structures that open and close with the heartbeat to regulate the one-way flow of blood through the heart.
They are muscular layers of the heart wall that generate the force needed to pump blood to the lungs.
They are receptors in the veins that sense pressure changes and trigger contraction of the cardiac muscle.
A.explain: Heart valves open and close with the heartbeat to maintain one-way blood flow. Septa partition chambers, myocardium generates force, and venous receptors sense pressure; none of these are valves.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes valves in veins?
options: They lie continuously along the lining of veins, especially in the arms, and push blood away from the heart.
They lie at intervals in the lining of veins, especially in the neck, and stop blood from reaching the heart.
They lie at intervals in the lining of veins, especially in the legs, and help move blood returning to the heart.
They lie only where veins join the heart chambers, especially the atria, and regulate one-way flow out of the heart.
A.explain: Venous valves occur at intervals in the lining of veins, particularly in the legs, and assist the return of blood to the heart. A continuous layer in the arms, valves that stop blood reaching the heart, or valves only at the heart chambers give the wrong place or the wrong job.

A.q: Which event immediately follows contraction of the right atrium?
options: The aortic valve opens and blood enters the aorta from the left ventricle
The pulmonary valve opens and blood enters the pulmonary artery from the right ventricle
The mitral valve opens and blood enters the left ventricle from the left atrium
The tricuspid valve opens and blood enters the right ventricle from the right atrium
A.explain: Contraction of the right atrium opens the tricuspid valve so blood passes into the right ventricle. The pulmonary semilunar valve opens after right ventricular contraction, while the mitral and aortic valves belong to the left side of the heart.

A.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?
options: The pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
The pulmonary vein, which carries oxygenated blood from the lungs.
The aorta, which carries oxygenated blood to all parts of the body.
The coronary vein, which returns deoxygenated blood from the myocardium.
A.explain: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood to the left atrium, the aorta carries oxygenated blood to the body, and coronary veins return deoxygenated blood from the heart muscle.

A.q: Which vessel returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium?
options: The superior vena cava, which returns deoxygenated blood from the body
The pulmonary vein, which returns oxygenated blood back from the lungs
The pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs
The aorta, which carries oxygenated blood to all parts of the body
A.explain: The pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the body, the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the aorta distributes oxygenated blood systemically.

A.q: Which chamber receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body?
options: Left atrium, which receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins
Left ventricle, which pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and body
Right atrium, which receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae
Right ventricle, which pumps deoxygenated blood to the pulmonary artery
A.explain: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae. The left atrium receives oxygenated pulmonary venous blood, the left ventricle ejects into the aorta, and the right ventricle ejects into the pulmonary artery.

A.q: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation?
options: Right atrium, which receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae
Right ventricle, which pumps deoxygenated blood to the pulmonary artery
Left atrium, which receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins
Left ventricle, which pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and body
A.explain: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta for systemic circulation. The right atrium receives venous blood, the right ventricle sends blood to the lungs, and the left atrium receives pulmonary venous blood.

A.q: What is the circulation of blood between the heart and its muscle tissue called?
A.explain: Coronary circulation is blood flow between the heart and its own muscular wall, through the right and left coronary arteries. Systemic circulation serves the body tissues, and pulmonary circulation serves the lungs.

A.q: Which set consists entirely of combining forms that mean vessel?
A.explain: Angi/o, Vas/o, and Vascul/o all mean vessel, as in angiogram, vasospasm, and vasculopathy. Aort/o names the aorta, Arteri/o an artery, Ven/o a vein, Cardi/o the heart, My/o muscle, Atri/o atrium, Coron/o circle or crown, Sphygm/o pulse, and Thromb/o clot, so those sets mix structures rather than the general vessel sense.

A.q: Which two combining forms both mean chest?
A.explain: Pector/o and Steth/o both mean chest, as in pectoral and stethoscope. Aort/o and Arteri/o name great vessels, My/o and Cardi/o name muscle and heart, and Ven/o and Phleb/o name vein.

A.q: In the term myocardial, the element myo refers to which structure?
options: Heart, as the pumping organ of the circulation
Vessel, as the tube that carries the blood
Chest, as the cavity that contains the heart
Muscle, as the middle layer of the heart wall
A.explain: In myocardial, myo means muscle, referring to the middle muscular layer of the heart wall. The heart sense belongs to cardi/o, the vessel sense to angi/o or vas/o, and the chest sense to pector/o or steth/o.

A.q: In the term cardioangiology, the element cardio refers to which structure?
options: Heart, as the muscular organ that pumps blood
Vessel, as the tube that carries blood to tissues
Atrium, as the upper chamber receiving venous blood
Chest, as the body region containing the heart
A.explain: In cardioangiology, cardio means heart, while angi/o means vessel. The term concerns heart and vessels, not the atrium or chest alone.

A.q: In the term atherosclerosis, the element ather refers to which substance?
options: Clot, as a mass formed within flowing blood
Fatty or lipid paste, as vessel wall material
Pulse, as the pressure wave felt in an artery
Vein, as a vessel returning blood toward the heart
A.explain: In atherosclerosis, ather means fatty or lipid paste, and the term describes hardening associated with fatty material in vessel walls. Clot is thromb/o, pulse is sphygm/o, and vein is ven/o or phleb/o.

A.q: In the term sphygmomanometer, the element sphygm refers to what?
options: Clot, as a mass formed within flowing blood
Vessel, as the tube that carries blood through body
Pulse, as the arterial pressure wave measured
Heart, as the muscular organ that pumps blood
A.explain: In sphygmomanometer, sphygm means pulse, and the device measures arterial pressure. Clot, vessel, and heart are named by other forms and are not the element carried by sphygm.

A.q: In the term varicose veins, the element varic refers to what?
options: A normal vein returning blood to the heart
A fatty deposit within an arterial wall
A clot forming inside a damaged vessel
A swollen or twisted vein, usually in legs
A.explain: In varicose veins, varic means swollen or twisted vein, and the suffix ose conveys full of. A normal vein, fatty deposit, and clot are named by ven/o, ather/o, and thromb/o, not by varic/o.

A.q: Which structure is the partition between the two upper chambers of the heart?
A.explain: The inter-atrial septum is the partition between the right and left atria. The inter-ventricular septum separates the ventricles, the pericardial cavity is the fluid-filled space around the heart, and the atrioventricular valve lies between an atrium and a ventricle.

A.q: Which structure is the partition between the right and left ventricles?
A.explain: The inter-ventricular septum is the partition between the right and left ventricles. The inter-atrial septum separates the atria, the pericardial cavity is the fluid-filled space around the heart, and a semilunar valve guards the outflow of a ventricle.

A.q: Which layer is the outer layer of the heart wall?
A.explain: The epicardium is the outer layer of the heart wall. The myocardium is the middle muscular layer, the endocardium is the inner lining, and the pericardium is the protective sac that encloses the heart rather than a wall layer.

A.q: What is the heart's muscular tissue called?
A.explain: The myocardium is the middle muscular layer of the heart wall, the tissue that contracts. The epicardium is the outer layer, the endocardium is the inner lining, and the pericardium is the protective sac around the heart rather than a wall muscle.

A.q: Which layer is the inner lining of the heart wall?
A.explain: The endocardium is the inner lining of the heart wall. The epicardium is the outer layer, the myocardium is the middle muscular layer, and the pericardium is the protective sac around the heart.

A.q: Which layer of the pericardium lies closest to the heart?
A.explain: The visceral pericardium is the layer closest to the heart, corresponding to the epicardium. The parietal pericardium is the outer wall layer, the fibrous pericardium is part of the outer sac, and the pericardial cavity is the fluid-filled space between the layers.

A.q: Which layer of the pericardium forms the outer wall of the sac?
A.explain: The parietal pericardium is the outer layer of the pericardial sac, pertaining to the wall. The visceral pericardium is the layer closest to the heart, while the myocardium and endocardium are heart wall layers rather than pericardial layers.

A.q: What is the pericardial cavity?
options: The fluid-filled space between parietal and visceral layers
The muscular chamber that pumps blood out into the aorta
The inner lining that covers the chambers and the valves
The partition that divides the two upper heart chambers
A.explain: The pericardial cavity is the fluid-filled space between the parietal and visceral layers of the pericardium. The chamber that pumps into the aorta is the left ventricle, the inner lining of the chambers is the endocardium, and the partition between the upper chambers is the inter-atrial septum.

A.q: Which valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
A.explain: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle. The bicuspid or mitral valve is between the left atrium and left ventricle, the pulmonary semilunar valve is between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery, and the aortic valve is between the left ventricle and aorta.

A.q: Which valve lies between the right ventricle and the artery leading to the lungs?
A.explain: The pulmonary semilunar valve lies between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery. The tricuspid valve is between the right atrium and right ventricle, the bicuspid or mitral valve is between the left atrium and left ventricle, and the aortic valve is between the left ventricle and aorta.

A.q: Which valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
A.explain: The bicuspid or mitral valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is between the right atrium and right ventricle, the pulmonary semilunar valve is between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery, and the aortic valve is between the left ventricle and aorta.

A.q: Which valve lies between the left ventricle and the aorta?
A.explain: The aortic valve lies between the left ventricle and the aorta. The tricuspid valve is between the right atrium and right ventricle, the pulmonary semilunar valve is between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery, and the bicuspid or mitral valve is between the left atrium and left ventricle.

A.q: The tricuspid valve takes its name from cuspis, and the pulmonary semilunar valve from luna. Which pairing of element to meaning is correct?
options: Cuspis means moon, and luna means point.
Cuspis means point, and luna means moon.
Cuspis means three, and luna means half.
Cuspis means valve, and luna means artery.
A.explain: Cuspis means point, which is why the tricuspid valve is named for its pointed leaflets, and luna means moon, which is why the pulmonary semilunar valve is named for its half-moon cusps. Pairing cuspis with moon and luna with point reverses the two roots. Pairing cuspis with three and luna with half, or cuspis with valve and luna with artery, assigns senses those roots do not carry.

A.q: Which vessels bring deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium?
options: The pulmonary veins from the lungs
The coronary arteries of the heart wall
The superior and inferior venae cavae
The aorta and its systemic branches
A.explain: The superior and inferior venae cavae bring deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium. The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs, the coronary arteries supply the heart muscle, and the aorta carries oxygenated blood out to the body.

A.q: What does the combining form Angi/o mean?
A.explain: Angi/o means vessel, as in angiogram. Aorta is Aort/o, artery is Arteri/o, and vein is Ven/o or Phleb/o.

A.q: What does the combining form Aort/o mean?
options: The aorta, the main trunk leaving the right ventricle
The aorta, the main trunk leaving the left ventricle
The aorta, the main vessel draining into the right atrium
The aorta, the main vessel carrying blood to the lungs
A.explain: Aort/o means the aorta, the main trunk leaving the left ventricle, as in aortalgia. The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs through the pulmonary trunk, and the venae cavae drain into the right atrium.

A.q: What does the combining form Arteri/o mean?
options: An artery, a vessel carrying blood back to the heart
An artery, a vessel draining lymph from the tissues
An artery, a vessel carrying blood away from the heart
An artery, a vessel with valves that stop backflow
A.explain: Arteri/o means artery, a vessel carrying blood away from the heart, as in arteriostenosis. Veins return blood to the heart and carry the valves that stop backflow, and lymphatic vessels drain lymph.

A.q: What does the combining form Atri/o mean?
options: The atrium, an upper chamber that receives blood
The atrium, a lower chamber that pumps blood out
The atrium, a lower chamber with the thickest wall
The atrium, a chamber that pumps blood to the body
A.explain: Atri/o means atrium, an upper heart chamber that receives blood, as in atrioventricular. The lower chambers, the ventricles, pump blood out, and the left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps blood to the body.

A.q: What does the combining form Coron/o mean?
A.explain: Coron/o means circle or crown, which is why the coronary arteries encircle the heart. Valve and septum are structural terms, and chamber is named by Atri/o or Ventricul/o.

A.q: What do the combining forms Pector/o and Steth/o both mean?
A.explain: Pector/o and Steth/o both mean chest, as in pectoral and stethoscope. Heart is Cardi/o, pulse is Sphygm/o, and clot is Thromb/o.

A.q: What is the combining form which means pulse?
A.explain: Sphygm/o means pulse, as in sphygmomanometer, the instrument that measures arterial pressure. Steth/o and Pector/o both mean chest, and Arteri/o means artery.

A.q: What is the combining form meaning clot?
A.explain: Thromb/o means clot, as in thrombosis, the condition in which a clot forms in a vessel. Pulse is Sphygm/o, muscle is My/o, and heart is Cardi/o.

A.q: What do the combining forms Ven/o and Phleb/o both mean?
A.explain: Ven/o and Phleb/o both mean vein, as in venosclerosis and phlebitis. Artery is Arteri/o, the aorta is Aort/o, and the ventricle is Ventricul/o.

A.q: The term phlebotomist comes from the combining form __________________ meaning _________________.
A.explain: Phlebotomist is built from phleb/o, which means vein, plus tom/o (to cut) and -ist (one who specializes). Ven/o is the other combining form for vein. Artery is arteri/o, and clot is thromb/o.

A.q: What is the combining form for ventricle?
A.explain: Ventricul/o means ventricle or pouch, the lower heart chamber, as in ventriculoatriostomy. The atrium is Atri/o, the aorta is Aort/o, and a valve is named by other terms.

A.q: Formed from angi/o, an ______________ is an x-ray record of a blood vessel.
A.explain: Angiogram is built from angi/o (vessel) and -gram (record), so it is an x-ray record of a blood vessel. A cardiograph records the heart, angioplasty is surgical repair of a vessel, and angiogenesis is the formation of new vessels.

A.q: What does the term vasospasm mean?
options: A clot forming inside a vessel
An involuntary contraction of a vessel
A surgical opening made in a vessel
A recorded image made of a vessel
A.explain: Vasospasm is built from Vas/o (vessel) and spasm (involuntary contraction), so it denotes an involuntary contraction of a vessel. A clot is thrombosis, a surgical opening uses -stomy, and a record uses -gram.

A.q: What does the term vasculopathy mean?
options: A surgical repair of a vessel
A.explain: Vasculopathy is built from Vascul/o (vessel) and -pathy (disease), so it denotes a disease of vessels. A record would use -gram, inflammation would use -itis, and surgical repair would use -plasty.

A.q: What does the term aortalgia mean?
A.explain: Aortalgia is built from Aort/o (aorta) and -algia (pain), so it denotes pain in the aorta. Inflammation would use -itis, narrowing would use -stenosis, and a record would use -gram.

A.q: What does the term arteriostenosis mean?
options: A surgical opening in an artery
A.explain: Arteriostenosis is built from Arteri/o (artery) and -stenosis (narrowing), so it denotes a narrowing of an artery. Pain would use -algia, a surgical opening would use -stomy, and inflammation would use -itis.

A.q: What is the meaning of atherosclerosis?
options: Inflammation of the veins along their course
Hardening of the arteries due to fatty deposits
Narrowing of the heart valves at the outlets
Enlargement of the heart muscle in the wall
A.explain: Atherosclerosis is built from ather/o (fatty or lipid paste) and -sclerosis (hardening), so it means hardening of the arteries due to fatty deposits. Inflammation of veins uses phleb/o with -itis, narrowing of valves is a stenotic valve lesion, and enlargement of heart muscle is hypertrophy of the myocardium.

A.q: What does the term atherectomy mean?
options: A record of fatty deposits in a vessel
Surgical removal of fatty plaque from a vessel
Inflammation of fatty tissue in a vessel
Narrowing caused by fatty deposits in a vessel
A.explain: Atherectomy is built from Athero (fatty or lipid paste) and -ectomy (surgical removal), so it denotes surgical removal of fatty plaque from a vessel. A record uses -gram, inflammation uses -itis, and narrowing uses -stenosis.

A.q: What does the term atrioventricular mean?
options: Pertaining to an atrium and a ventricle
Pertaining to the aorta and a ventricle
Pertaining to a vein and an artery
Pertaining to the heart and the chest
A.explain: Atrioventricular is built from Atri/o (atrium) and ventricul/o (ventricle) with -ar (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to an atrium and a ventricle. The other options pair structures that are not named together in this term.

A.q: What does the term cardioangiology mean?
options: The study of the heart and vessels
The study of the heart and lungs
The study of the chest and muscles
The study of blood and clots
A.explain: Cardioangiology is built from Cardi/o (heart), Angi/o (vessel), and -logy (study), so it denotes the study of the heart and vessels. The lungs, chest muscles, blood, and clots are named by other forms, none of which appears here.

A.q: The _________________ arteries are so named because they seem to encircle the heart like a crown.
A.explain: Coronary is built from coron/o, which means circle or crown, and -ary, pertaining to. The right and left coronary arteries encircle the heart and supply its muscle.

A.q: What does the term myocardial mean?
A.explain: Myocardial is built from My/o (muscle) and cardi/o (heart) with -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the heart muscle. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term pectoral mean?
A.explain: Pectoral is built from Pector/o (chest) and -al (pertaining to), so it means pertaining to the chest. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term stethoscope mean?
options: An instrument for examining the chest
An instrument for measuring the pulse
An instrument for recording the heart
An instrument for opening a vessel
A.explain: Stethoscope is built from Steth/o (chest) and -scope (instrument for examining), so it denotes an instrument for examining the chest. Measuring the pulse uses Sphygm/o, recording the heart uses Cardi/o with -graph, and opening a vessel uses Vas/o with -stomy.

A.q: What does the term sphygmomanometer mean?
options: An instrument for recording the sounds of the heart
An instrument for measuring pulse or blood pressure
An instrument for examining the chest wall
An instrument for opening a closed vessel
A.explain: Sphygmomanometer is built from Sphygm/o (pulse), man/o (pressure), and -meter (measuring instrument), so it denotes a pressure-measuring instrument, the blood pressure cuff. Recording the heart uses Cardi/o with -graph, examining the chest uses Steth/o with -scope, and opening a vessel uses Vas/o with -stomy.

A.q: What does the term thrombosis mean?
options: An inflammation of a vein caused by a clot
A condition in which a clot forms in a vessel
Surgical removal of a clot from a vessel
A recorded image of a clot inside a vessel
A.explain: Thrombosis is built from Thromb/o (clot) and -osis (condition), so it denotes the condition in which a clot forms within a vessel. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What is the meaning of thrombocyte?
A.explain: Thrombocyte is built from thromb/o (clot) and -cyte (cell), so it is a cell involved in clotting. Formation of a clot is thrombosis, destruction of a clot is thrombolysis, and inflammation of a clotted vein is thrombophlebitis.

A.q: What does the term venosclerosis mean?
options: A surgical removal of a vein
A.explain: Venosclerosis is built from Ven/o (vein) and -sclerosis (hardening), so it denotes a hardening of a vein. Widening would use -ectasis, a clot would use Thromb/o, and surgical removal would use -ectomy.

A.q: What does the term varicose veins mean?
options: Veins that are narrowed and hardened inside.
Veins that are swollen or twisted in the legs.
Veins that are blocked by a clot inside them.
Veins that are inflamed by a local infection.
A.explain: Varicose veins is built from Varic/o (swollen or twisted vein) and -ose (full of), so it denotes veins that are swollen or twisted, usually in the legs. Narrowed and hardened veins are venosclerosis, a blocking clot is thrombosis, and inflammation uses -itis.

A.q: What does the term ventriculoatriostomy mean?
options: A surgical opening between a ventricle and an atrium
A recorded X-ray image of a ventricle and an atrium
An inflammation of a ventricle and an atrium
A narrowing between a ventricle and an atrium
A.explain: Ventriculoatriostomy is built from Ventricul/o (ventricle), Atri/o (atrium), and -stomy (surgical opening), so it denotes a surgical opening between a ventricle and an atrium. A record uses -gram, inflammation uses -itis, and narrowing uses -stenosis.

A.q: Match each heart valve to the flow it guards.

rightItems.text: Guards the outlet from the left ventricle into the systemic trunk
Guards the inlet from the right atrium into the right ventricle
Guards the outlet from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk
Guards the inlet from the left atrium into the left ventricle
Guards the return from the body veins into the right atrium

A.explain: The tricuspid valve guards flow from the right atrium into the right ventricle, the pulmonary semilunar valve guards flow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk, the bicuspid or mitral valve guards flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle, and the aortic valve guards flow from the left ventricle into the aorta. The return from the body veins into the right atrium is the vena caval inlet, which none of these four valves guards.

A.q: Match each type of circulation to the path it describes.

rightItems.text: Flow between the heart and the body tissues
Flow between the heart and the gas exchange organs
Flow between the heart and its own muscular wall
Flow between the atria across the dividing septum

A.explain: Systemic circulation is flow between the heart and the body tissues, pulmonary circulation is flow between the heart and the lungs, and coronary circulation is flow between the heart and its own muscular wall. Flow across the inter-atrial septum is not a named circulation: the septum partitions the atria rather than carrying a circuit.

A.q: Match each suffix to the meaning it adds in a cardiovascular term.

rightItems.text: Record or image
Narrowing of a passage
Surgical removal
Pain
Surgical opening
Hardening of tissue
Inflammation of a structure

A.explain: -gram means a record or image, -stenosis means narrowing, -ectomy means surgical removal, -algia means pain, -stomy means a surgical opening, and -sclerosis means hardening. Inflammation is the sense of -itis, which is not among these suffixes, so that line matches none of them.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or idea it denotes.

rightItems.text: Upper heart chamber
Main trunk leaving the left ventricle
Vessel carrying blood away from the heart
Ring or wreath

A.explain: Aort/o means aorta, the main trunk leaving the left ventricle. Arteri/o means artery, a vessel carrying blood away from the heart. Coron/o means circle or crown, giving coronary its sense of encircling the heart. Atri/o means atrium, an upper heart chamber.

A.q: Match each remaining combining form to the structure or idea it denotes.

rightItems.text: Lower heart chamber or pouch
Vessel returning blood to the heart
Mass formed in flowing blood
Pulse wave felt in an artery
Fatty or lipid paste
Swollen or twisted vein

A.explain: Thromb/o means clot, a mass formed in flowing blood. Ven/o and Phleb/o mean vein, a vessel returning blood to the heart. Ventricul/o means ventricle or pouch, the lower heart chamber. Varic/o means a swollen or twisted vein. Athero means fatty or lipid paste. Sphygm/o means pulse, the pressure wave felt in an artery.

A.q: Which name is also used for the atria?
options: Auricles, the upper right and left chambers
Ventricles, the lower right and left chambers
Septa, the partitions between the two sides
Cusps, the pointed leaflets of the inlet valves
A.explain: The atria are also called auricles, and they are the upper right and left chambers. Ventricles are the lower chambers, septa are the partitions between the sides, and cusps are the pointed leaflets of the atrioventricular valves.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the ventricles?
options: They are the upper right and left chambers of the heart.
They are the lower right and left chambers of the heart.
They are the valves between the atria and the ventricles.
They are the septa that partition the right and left sides.
A.explain: The ventricles are the lower right and left chambers of the heart. The upper chambers are the atria, the valves between atria and ventricles are the atrioventricular valves, and the septa are the partitions between the right and left sides.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the flow of oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart?
options: It returns through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium, then through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
It returns through the pulmonary artery into the right atrium, then through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
It returns through the superior vena cava into the right atrium, then through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
It returns through the aorta into the left atrium, then through the aortic valve into the left ventricle.
A.explain: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium, and contraction of the left atrium opens the mitral or bicuspid valve so blood flows into the left ventricle. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, the superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the body, and the aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle rather than returning it to the left atrium.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the flow of blood from the left ventricle into the systemic circulation?
options: Contraction of the left ventricle opens the aortic valve and blood flows into the aorta and to all parts of the body
Contraction of the left ventricle opens the pulmonary semilunar valve and blood flows into the pulmonary artery and lungs
Contraction of the left ventricle opens the tricuspid valve and blood flows back into the right atrium
Contraction of the left ventricle opens the mitral valve and blood flows back into the left atrium
A.explain: Contraction of the left ventricle opens the aortic valve and blood flows into the aorta and to all parts of the body, which is the systemic circulation. The pulmonary semilunar valve is the right ventricular outlet, and the tricuspid and mitral valves are inlet valves rather than outlets from the left ventricle.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the flow of blood out of the right ventricle?
options: Contraction of the right ventricle opens the pulmonary valve and blood flows to the lungs by the pulmonary artery
Contraction of the right ventricle opens the aortic valve and blood flows into the aorta and onward to the body
Contraction of the right ventricle opens the mitral valve and blood flows across the heart into the left atrium
Contraction of the right ventricle opens the tricuspid valve and blood flows backward into the right atrium again
A.explain: Contraction of the right ventricle opens the pulmonary valve, and blood flows to the lungs by the pulmonary artery, where it is oxygenated. The aortic valve is the left ventricular outlet, and the mitral and tricuspid valves are inlet valves rather than outlets from the right ventricle.

A.q: This upper chamber receives the venae cavae. Answer each step, then the next chamber follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this chamber?
Which valve borders the Right atrium?
Where does the other atrium lie relative to the Right atrium?
Where does the ventricle it feeds lie?
options: On the opposite side of the chest

steps.prompt: What lies on its medial side?

A.explain: This upper chamber is the right atrium, also called an auricle. The tricuspid valve is its outlet into the right ventricle. The left atrium lies to its left, the right ventricle lies inferior to it, and the inter-atrial septum is medial. Mitral, pulmonary semilunar, and aortic name other borders. To its right is the side of the other atrium, not this one. Superior to it is not where its ventricle lies. The aortic valve, the pericardial cavity, and the pulmonary vein are not the medial partition.

A.q: This upper chamber receives the pulmonary veins. Answer each step, then the next chamber follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this chamber?
Which valve borders the Left atrium?
Where does the other atrium lie relative to the Left atrium?
Where does the ventricle it feeds lie?
options: On the opposite side of the chest

steps.prompt: What lies on its medial side?

A.explain: This upper chamber is the left atrium, also called an auricle. The mitral valve is its outlet into the left ventricle. The right atrium lies to its right, the left ventricle lies inferior to it, and the inter-atrial septum is medial. Tricuspid, pulmonary semilunar, and aortic name other borders. To its left is not the side of the other atrium. Superior to it is not where its ventricle lies. The pulmonary semilunar valve, the pericardial cavity, and the vena cava are not the medial partition.

A.q: This lower chamber receives blood through the tricuspid opening from the chamber above it. Answer each step, then the next chamber follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this chamber?
Which valve is its inlet?
Which valve is its outlet?
Where does the atrium that feeds it lie?
options: On the left side of the heart

steps.prompt: Where does the other ventricle lie relative to the Right ventricle?

A.explain: This lower chamber is the right ventricle. The tricuspid valve is the inlet from the right atrium, and the pulmonary semilunar valve is the outlet into the pulmonary artery. The right atrium lies superior to it. The left ventricle lies to its left, with the inter-ventricular septum medial. Mitral and aortic are left-sided valves. Inferior to it is not where its atrium lies. To its right is not the side of the other ventricle.

A.q: This lower chamber sends blood into the aorta. Answer each step, then the valve run follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this chamber?
Which valve is its inlet?
Which valve is its outlet?
Where does the atrium that feeds it lie?
options: On the right side of the heart

steps.prompt: Where does the other ventricle lie relative to the Left ventricle?

A.explain: This lower chamber is the left ventricle. The mitral valve is the inlet from the left atrium, and the aortic valve is the outlet into the aorta. The left atrium lies superior to it. The right ventricle lies to its right. Tricuspid and pulmonary semilunar are right-sided valves. Inferior to it is not where its atrium lies. To its left is not the side of the other ventricle.

A.q: This valve stands between the right atrium and the right ventricle. Answer each step, then the next valve follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this valve?
Which role is the Tricuspid valve?
Where does the atrium lie relative to the Tricuspid valve?
options: On the left side of the heart

steps.prompt: Where does the ventricle lie relative to the Tricuspid valve?
options: On the left side of the heart

A.explain: This is the tricuspid valve, the right inlet. The right atrium lies superior to it and the right ventricle lies inferior to it. Outlet valve is the opposite role. Inferior to it is not where the atrium lies, and superior to it is not where the ventricle lies. The left side of the heart is the mitral and aortic side.

A.q: This half-moon valve on the right side of the heart opens toward the lungs. Answer each step, then the next valve follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this valve?
Which role is the Pulmonary semilunar valve?
Which chamber lies inferior to the Pulmonary semilunar valve?
Which vessel leaves through the Pulmonary semilunar valve?

A.explain: This is the pulmonary semilunar valve, the right outlet. The right ventricle lies inferior to it, and the pulmonary artery leaves through it. Inlet valve is the opposite role. Left ventricle, right atrium, and left atrium meet other valves. The aorta, pulmonary vein, and vena cava meet other chambers.

A.q: This valve stands between the left atrium and the left ventricle. Answer each step, then the next valve follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this valve?
Which other name belongs to the Mitral valve?
Which role is the Mitral valve?
Where does the ventricle lie relative to the Mitral valve?
options: On the right side of the heart

A.explain: This is the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve, the left inlet. The left ventricle lies inferior to it. Tricuspid valve, semilunar valve, and coronary valve name other structures. Outlet valve is the opposite role. Superior to it is not where the ventricle lies, and the right side of the heart is not this border.

A.q: This half-moon valve on the left side of the heart opens toward the body. Answer each step, then the vessel run follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this valve?
Which role is the Aortic valve?
Which chamber lies inferior to the Aortic valve?
Which vessel leaves through the Aortic valve?

A.explain: This is the aortic valve, the left outlet. The left ventricle lies inferior to it, and the aorta leaves through it. Inlet valve is the opposite role. Right ventricle, left atrium, and right atrium meet other valves. The pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, and vena cava meet other chambers.

A.q: This vessel links the heart to the lungs and has thick, muscular walls. Answer each step, then the next vessel follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this vessel?
Which direction does the Pulmonary artery run?
Which blood does the Pulmonary artery carry?
Which chamber does the Pulmonary artery leave?

A.explain: This is the pulmonary artery. It runs away from the heart, carries deoxygenated blood, and leaves the right ventricle. Toward the heart is the direction of the pulmonary veins and the venae cavae. Oxygenated blood in a vessel leaving the heart is the aorta. The left atrium receives the pulmonary veins, the left ventricle feeds the aorta, and the right atrium receives the venae cavae.

A.q: This vessel is one of four that join the lungs and the heart. Answer each step, then the next vessel follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this vessel?
Which direction does the Pulmonary vein run?
Which blood does the Pulmonary vein carry?
Which chamber does the Pulmonary vein enter?

A.explain: This is the pulmonary vein. It runs toward the heart, carries oxygenated blood, and enters the left atrium. Away from the heart is the direction of the pulmonary artery and the aorta. Deoxygenated blood returning to the heart arrives by the venae cavae. The right ventricle feeds the pulmonary artery, the left ventricle feeds the aorta, and the right atrium receives the venae cavae.

A.q: This is the largest vessel in the body. Answer each step, then the next vessel follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this vessel?
Which direction does the Aorta run?
Which blood does the Aorta carry?
Which chamber does the Aorta leave?

A.explain: This is the aorta. It runs away from the heart, carries oxygenated blood, and leaves the left ventricle. Toward the heart is the direction of the pulmonary veins and the venae cavae. Deoxygenated blood leaving the heart is the pulmonary artery. The right ventricle feeds the pulmonary artery, the left atrium receives the pulmonary veins, and the right atrium receives the venae cavae.

A.q: These two large vessels, one superior and one inferior, are named for their hollow shape. Answer each step, then the next vessel follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this vessel?
Which direction does the Vena cava run?
Which blood does the Vena cava carry?
Which chamber does the Vena cava enter?

A.explain: This is the vena cava. Venae cava moves the plural onto the first word, Vena cavae moves it onto the second, and Venae cavae is the plural pair, not the singular vessel asked here. It runs toward the heart, carries deoxygenated blood, and enters the right atrium. Away from the heart is the direction of the aorta and the pulmonary artery. Oxygenated blood returning to the heart arrives by the pulmonary veins. The left atrium receives those veins, and the ventricles are the pumping chambers rather than this inlet.

A.q: These arteries branch from the aorta just above its valve. Answer each step, then the wall cluster follows.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of these arteries?
Which sense gives these arteries their name?
Which tissue do these arteries supply?
Which circulation do these arteries serve?

A.explain: These are the coronary arteries, named from coron/o, circle or crown. They supply the heart muscle, which is coronary circulation. Fatty paste is athero, a clot is thromb/o, and a pulse is sphygm/o. Lung tissue is the pulmonary path, body tissues are the systemic path, and venous valves are not the tissue these arteries supply. Septal circulation is not a named circuit.

A.q: Which layer belongs at each depth of the heart wall? At each step, choose, then continue.

steps.prompt: Outer layer
Middle muscle
Inner lining

A.explain: From outer to inner the wall is epicardium, myocardium, endocardium. The myocardium is the muscle. The pericardium is the sac around the heart, not a wall layer. Epicardium is not the middle or inner layer, myocardium is not the outer or inner layer, and endocardium is not the outer or middle layer.

A.q: Which part of the pericardium is being named? At each step, choose, then continue.

steps.prompt: Layer closest to the heart
Outer wall of the sac
Fluid space between the layers

A.explain: The visceral pericardium lies closest to the heart and corresponds to the epicardium. The parietal pericardium forms the outer wall of the sac. The pericardial cavity is the fluid space between them. Myocardium and endocardium are wall layers, not parts of the sac. Parietal is not the layer closest to the heart, and visceral is not the outer wall.

A.q: Which path belongs to each circulation? At each step, choose, then continue.

steps.prompt: Systemic circulation
Pulmonary circulation
Coronary circulation

A.explain: Systemic circulation runs between the heart and the body tissues. Pulmonary circulation runs between the heart and the lungs. Coronary circulation runs between the heart and its own muscle. Flow across the septum is not a circulation. The septum partitions the sides. Heart and lungs is not the systemic path, heart and body tissues is not the pulmonary path, and neither of those is the coronary path.

A.q: Label each step of blood flow through the heart, lungs and body.
A.alt: Circular flow diagram with arrows showing the path of blood: from the body tissues through the right side of the heart to the lungs, then back through the left side of the heart to the aorta and body. All 14 step labels are blank.
A.explain: Deoxygenated blood returns from the body tissues through the vena cava into the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, and is pumped through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta and out to the body tissues.

A.q: Label the structures of the heart.
A.alt: Cutaway front view of the heart showing its four chambers, valves, septa, great vessels and wall layers, with 21 blank labels connected to the structures by leader lines.
A.explain: The right atrium receives blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and sends it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery. The left atrium receives blood from the pulmonary veins and sends it through the mitral (bicuspid) valve to the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta and aortic arch. The interatrial and interventricular septa separate the right and left sides. From the inside out, the wall layers are the endocardium, myocardium and epicardium, and the pericardium surrounds the heart.

A.q: Label the parts of the heart's electrical conduction system.
A.alt: Cutaway drawing of the heart with the conduction system highlighted: the SA node in the right atrium, internodal pathways, the AV node, the bundle of His, the right and left bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers in the ventricle walls. The four chambers are also marked. All 11 labels are blank.
A.credit: "Heart and electrical conduction system" by Drj (CardioNetworks), blank version by YitzhakNat; CC BY-SA 3.0; via Wikimedia Commons. Leader lines and blank label areas added.
A.explain: Each heartbeat starts at the sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart's natural pacemaker in the right atrium. The impulse spreads across the atria and along the internodal pathways to the atrioventricular (AV) node, which delays it briefly so the ventricles can fill. It then travels down the bundle of His, splits into the right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum, and spreads through the Purkinje fibers so the ventricles contract from the apex upward.

A.q: Label the coronary arteries and the surrounding structures of the heart.
A.alt: Front view of the heart showing the right coronary artery and the left coronary artery with its branches on the heart's surface, along with the great vessels and chambers. All 14 labels are blank.
A.credit: "Coronary arteries" by Patrick J. Lynch, Fred the Oyster, and Mikael Häggström; CC BY-SA 3.0; via Wikimedia Commons. Labels removed.
A.explain: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself. The right coronary artery runs along the right side and gives off the right marginal artery and, in most people, the posterior descending artery. The left coronary artery quickly divides into the left anterior descending artery (anterior interventricular artery), which gives off diagonal branches, and the circumflex artery, which gives off the left (obtuse) marginal arteries. A blockage in these vessels causes ischemia or a myocardial infarction (heart attack).

A.q: Label the parts of the blood vessels and the layers of the vessel wall.
A.alt: Diagram of an artery carrying blood from the heart, branching into arterioles, a capillary network and venules, which join a vein that returns blood to the heart. Cutaways show the layers of the artery wall and a valve inside the vein, and a close-up of a capillary shows a red blood cell. All 13 labels are blank.
A.credit: "Blood vessels" by Kelvinsong; CC BY-SA 3.0; via Wikimedia Commons. Labels removed.
A.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and branch into arterioles and then capillaries, where gases and nutrients are exchanged. Capillaries drain into venules, which join to form veins that carry blood back to the heart. Valves in veins prevent backflow. From the lumen outward, the artery wall is made of the endothelium (tunica intima), the internal elastic lamina, a smooth muscle layer (tunica media), the external elastic lamina, and the adventitia (tunica externa). Erythrocytes (red blood cells) pass through capillaries in single file.

A.title: Pulmonary Circulation
A.q: Pulmonary circulation: put the stages in the order blood flows from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the heart.
A.explain: Pulmonary circulation carries blood from the heart to the lungs and back. The right ventricle contracts and pushes deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary semilunar valve, which opens into the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary arteries carry that blood to the lungs, so they come before the lungs (some slides wrongly list the lungs before the pulmonary artery). In the lungs the blood picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. The pulmonary veins then carry the oxygenated blood back to the left atrium, where pulmonary circulation ends. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood, the opposite of the rest of the body.

A.title: Systemic Circulation
A.q: Systemic circulation: put the stages in the order blood flows from the left ventricle to the body and back to the heart.
A.explain: Systemic circulation carries blood from the heart to all parts of the body and back. The left ventricle contracts and pushes oxygenated blood through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta, the largest artery. The aorta and its branches deliver the blood to the body tissues, where oxygen is given up and carbon dioxide is picked up. The deoxygenated blood then returns through the superior and inferior vena cava to the right atrium, where systemic circulation ends.

A.title: Full Loop
A.q: Full loop: put the stages in the order blood flows from the body tissues, through both sides of the heart and the lungs, and out again in the aorta.
A.explain: Deoxygenated blood leaves the body tissues and returns through the vena cava into the right atrium. It passes the tricuspid AV valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary arteries carry the deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen. The pulmonary veins carry the oxygenated blood back to the left atrium. It passes the bicuspid AV valve (also called the mitral valve) into the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta and on to the body tissues again. The right side of the heart always handles deoxygenated blood and the left side oxygenated blood.

A.title: Heart Valves
A.q: Put the four heart valves in the order blood passes through them, starting from the right atrium.
A.explain: Blood meets the tricuspid AV valve first, between the right atrium and the right ventricle. Leaving the right ventricle, it passes the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary arteries. After the lungs it returns to the left atrium and passes the bicuspid AV valve, also called the mitral valve, into the left ventricle. Last, it leaves through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta. The AV (atrioventricular) valves sit between each atrium and ventricle, and the semilunar valves sit at the exits of the ventricles.

A.title: Heart Chambers
A.q: Put the four heart chambers in the order blood passes through them.
A.explain: Blood from the body enters the right atrium, then drops into the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. The oxygenated blood comes back through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then drops into the left ventricle, which pumps it out to the body. The atria receive blood, and the ventricles pump it out of the heart.

A.title: Coronary Circulation
A.q: Coronary circulation: put the stages in the order oxygenated blood reaches the heart muscle itself.
A.explain: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta. The first branches of the aorta, right at its root, are the right and left coronary arteries, so the heart is the first organ to receive oxygenated blood. The coronary arteries spread over the surface of the heart and supply the myocardium, the heart muscle itself, which needs a constant supply of oxygen to keep pumping.

A.q: Match each type of circulation to its description. One description stays unmatched.

rightItems.text: Carries blood from the heart to all parts of the body and back to the heart
Supplies the heart muscle itself through the right and left coronary arteries
Carries blood from the lungs straight to the body without passing through the heart
Carries blood from the heart to the lungs for oxygenation and back to the heart

A.explain: Pulmonary circulation carries blood from the heart to the lungs for oxygenation and back to the heart. Systemic circulation carries blood from the heart to all parts of the body and back to the heart. Coronary circulation supplies the heart muscle itself through the right and left coronary arteries. "Carries blood from the lungs straight to the body without passing through the heart" matches none of them: blood from the lungs always returns to the left atrium before the left ventricle pumps it to the body.

A.q: Follow the blood as it leaves the right ventricle. Answer each step.

steps.prompt: Leaving the right ventricle, which circulation does the blood enter first?
Back on the left side of the heart, which circulation does it enter next?
Which organ receives oxygenated blood first?

A.explain: From the right ventricle, blood enters pulmonary circulation: the pulmonary arteries take it to the lungs, and the pulmonary veins bring it back to the left atrium. From the left ventricle it enters systemic circulation through the aorta to the rest of the body. The first branches of the aorta are the right and left coronary arteries, so the heart is the first organ to receive oxygenated blood (coronary circulation). The lungs exchange gases but are not fed by the pulmonary veins, and the brain and body tissues are reached only after the coronary branches.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes which vessels carry deoxygenated and oxygenated blood in pulmonary and systemic circulation?
options: In pulmonary circulation the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins oxygenated blood; in systemic circulation the arteries carry oxygenated blood and the veins deoxygenated blood

In pulmonary circulation the pulmonary arteries carry oxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins deoxygenated blood; in systemic circulation the arteries carry deoxygenated blood and the veins oxygenated blood
In both pulmonary and systemic circulation every artery carries oxygenated blood and every vein carries deoxygenated blood, with no exceptions anywhere in the body at all
In pulmonary circulation both the pulmonary arteries and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood, and in systemic circulation only the vena cava carries deoxygenated blood
A.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it back, whatever its oxygen content. In pulmonary circulation the pulmonary arteries take deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood back to the left atrium. In systemic circulation the aorta and arteries carry oxygenated blood to the body, and the vena cava and veins return deoxygenated blood to the right atrium. "In pulmonary circulation the pulmonary arteries carry oxygenated blood…" swaps both circulations. "In both circulations every artery carries oxygenated blood…" ignores the pulmonary exception. "In pulmonary circulation both the pulmonary arteries and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood…" forgets that blood reaches the lungs deoxygenated.
